item.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot
item.description:
NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot

NVIDIA demonstrated an end‑to‑end workflow that uses RTX Spark, Isaac Lab, and Omniverse tools to create a simulated obstacle course, train a navigation policy for the Microduck robot, and evaluate the policy in Isaac Sim.

🔍 Overview

  • Teaching a robot to navigate an obstacle course requires perception, balance, and the ability to adjust actions when obstacles block the path ahead, not just a walking policy.
  • The development process links three stages: creating assets and an environment, using physics simulation to model robot‑environment interaction, and training + evaluating policies in simulation.

🛠️ Tools and Roles

Component Role
RTX Spark Local development hub; supports AI‑assisted planning, policy validation, and receives trained policies for local evaluation in Isaac Sim.
Isaac Lab Cloud‑based robot‑learning framework for reinforcement learning.
Newton Models physical behavior for simulation.
Omniverse libraries Generate simulated visual observations via RTX rendering.
Isaac Sim Runs local evaluation of trained policies returned from RTX Spark.
Hermes Translates prompts into step‑by‑step project plans and creates asset inventories from images.
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt Works with Hermes to generate project plans and analyze images for reusable assets.
Astra Builds and tests assets; directs FreeCAD geometry creation and Blender material application.
SimReady Central Library Free, ungated library of >2,000 simulation‑ready OpenUSD assets.
Microduck Reference quadruped robot used for navigation training.

📐 Workflow Steps

  1. Write a natural‑language prompt that describes the obstacle course and what Microduck must learn.
  2. On RTX Spark, Hermes and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt translate the prompt into a detailed project plan (task, resources, outputs, stages).
  3. Review official Microduck documentation and summarize its capabilities, constraints, and unknowns.
  4. Define the course layout, obstacle dimensions, clearances, and intended route.
  5. Generate a photorealistic concept image using a verified Microduck reference image.
  6. Hermes and Nemotron analyze the concept image, extract unique reusable assets, assign identifiers, and create cropped reference images.
  7. Astra enhances the references, models geometry in FreeCAD, and adds fine details and materials in Blender.
  8. Assemble the assets into a simulated environment; Newton provides physics, Omniverse renders visuals.
  9. Train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab in the cloud using the simulated environment.
  10. Return the trained policy to RTX Spark and evaluate it locally in Isaac Sim.
  11. Verify robot capabilities, test navigation, obstacle handling, and reset logic—all in simulation (no physical hardware).
  12. Package the plan, robot brief, concept, asset inventory, crops, and execution instructions for reproducibility.

📊 What You’ll Learn

  • How to create a simulated obstacle course for a quadruped robot.
  • How AI agents (Hermes, Nemotron, Astra) automate planning, asset extraction, and 3D modeling.
  • How to train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab and validate it with RTX Spark and Isaac Sim.
  • How to leverage the SimReady Central Library for reusable simulation assets.

#NVIDIA #Robotics #Simulation #ReinforcementLearning #AIAgents

Source: Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Skild AI launches S1, a video‑to‑robot foundation model for manipulation
item.description:
Skild AI launches S1, a video‑to‑robot foundation model for manipulation

🔍 Overview

Skild AI unveiled S1 in August 2026 as its flagship foundation model for robotic manipulation. The system can learn a new task from a single video demonstration without any additional task‑specific training or weight adjustments.

🧩 How S1 Works

  • The model receives a video showing a task and then attempts to replicate the observed task using a robot, without modifying its weights or requiring a specific post‑training phase.
  • S1 is trained using episodes in which a visual demonstration describes the task to be performed.
  • It learns to relate what it observes in the video to the current scene and the available motor controls, reconstructing an action policy that achieves the same goal with its own robotic body.
  • Pre‑training combines several data types: teleoperation, first‑person human videos, simulation, and experiments conducted on robots.
  • Several scenarios did not appear in the pre‑training data; basic gestures are combined into novel sequences.

📊 Performance Metrics

  • On unseen tasks lasting four to eight minutes, trained on a reported 100,000 hours of data, S1 achieved an average cumulative success rate per step of 66 %, compared with 9 % for a linguistic baseline.
  • The metric aggregates the success rates of the various stages; it does not represent a 66 % success rate for each mission.
  • Human intervention was used to reset the system after a failure so that all stages could be evaluated.
  • A real‑world demonstration is estimated to be equivalent to approximately 380 post‑training sessions on the tasks studied.

🛠️ Supporting Infrastructure

Component Role
Cosmos Organizes and enriches video data
Omniverse Provides virtual environments
Isaac Sim Provides virtual environments
Isaac Lab Used for reinforcement learning
TensorRT Optimizes inference

On September 10 2026 NVIDIA detailed this infrastructure, highlighting how Cosmos, Omniverse, Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, and TensorRT work together to train, simulate, and deploy S1.

🚀 Availability

  • S1 is available through select deployments and partnerships, not as a freely downloadable model.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Enables robots to acquire new manipulation skills from a single video, dramatically reducing the data collection and training time required for each new task.
  • Demonstrated capabilities include repotting a plant, making filter coffee, making pancakes, and assembling a kit, with sequences lasting up to ten minutes and involving several successive gestures.
  • For the repotting task, the company reports that it went from recording the demonstration to beginning autonomous execution in eleven minutes.
  • The same set of weights generates all the examples shown, confirming the model’s ability to generalize across diverse tasks.

#SkildAI #Robotics #FoundationModel #Simulation

Source: 5 Steps to Create SimReady Assets for Robotics with Frontier AI Models | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: Skild AI’s S1: Learning a Robotic Task from a Video

item.title: Introduction of SimLife Platform and SimLife-BP Behavioral Pattern Benchmark
item.description:
Introduction of SimLife Platform and SimLife-BP Behavioral Pattern Benchmark

Researchers have introduced SimLife, a scalable platform designed to simulate long-term household life, alongside a corresponding benchmark called SimLife-BP to evaluate long-context pattern understanding.

🔍 Overview

SimLife is a simulation platform that provides:

  • Rich visual observations
  • Ground-truth action logs
  • Synthetic dialogues with audio

⚙️ Key details

SimLife-BP is used to evaluate the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from observations spanning weeks or months. The benchmark consists of:

  • 106 episodes
  • 1,439 question-answer pairs
  • Average episode length of 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days

🧩 How it works

Tasks within the benchmark probe the following types of reasoning under various levels of rule hints:

  • Direct reasoning
  • Counterfactual reasoning
  • Noisy reasoning
  • Inverse reasoning

💡 Why it matters

Evaluations of frontier models and architectures revealed several limitations in current AI capabilities:

  • Models often achieve surface-level prediction instead of comprehensive rule understanding.
  • Models rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning based on evidence.
  • Models struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change.

#SimLife #AIbenchmarks #LongContext #BehavioralModeling

Source: SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership
